title: Fabius the Delayer
text:
In 217 BC Hannibal destroyed a Roman army at Lake Trasimene, and Rome in panic named Quintus Fabius Maximus dictator. Fabius decided not to fight Hannibal in open battle at all. Instead he followed the Carthaginian army along the hills, camping on high ground, cutting off foragers and stragglers, and denying Hannibal the decisive victory he needed. Hannibal was far from home, and every month without a battle wore his army down.

The strategy made Fabius hated. Plutarch says the soldiers called him Hannibal's pedagogue, the slave who trails after a child, and his own master of horse, Minucius, mocked him as a coward. Hannibal made it worse by sparing Fabius's estates while burning everything around them, to make him look like a traitor. The people gave Minucius equal command. Minucius soon attacked rashly and was trapped, and Fabius came down from the hills and saved him. Plutarch reports that Minucius then called Fabius father and put himself under his command again.

When Fabius's term ended, Rome returned to pitched battle, and in 216 BC lost a huge army at Cannae. After that disaster the Romans went back to his method of avoiding battle with Hannibal while wearing him down. The poet Ennius later wrote that one man, by delaying, restored the state, and Fabius kept the nickname Cunctator, the Delayer.
lesson: Against a stronger opponent who needs a quick win, refusing the fight he wants can be your best move. Expect to be called timid while it works.
people: Quintus Fabius Maximus, Marcus Minucius Rufus, Hannibal
source: Plutarch, Life of Fabius Maximus 5 to 13; Livy, History of Rome, book 22
